history.heading: Indigenous peoples and Spanish colonisation
paragraphs: Before European arrival, present-day Argentina was home to diverse peoples, including the Diaguita in the northwest, who were influenced by the Inca Empire, the Guaraní in the northeast, and nomadic hunter-gatherers in the Pampas and Patagonia, such as the Tehuelche.

Spanish explorers arrived in the early 16th century. Buenos Aires was founded in 1536 and again, permanently, in 1580. The region was a peripheral part of the Spanish Empire until 1776, when the Viceroyalty of the Río de la Plata was created with Buenos Aires as its capital.

history.heading: Independence and nation-building
paragraphs: The May Revolution of 1810 began the movement for independence, which was formally declared in Tucumán on 9 July 1816. General José de San Martín led armies across the Andes to help liberate Chile and Peru.

Decades of conflict between Buenos Aires and the provinces followed, including the rule of Juan Manuel de Rosas. A federal constitution was adopted in 1853. In the late 19th century, military campaigns known as the Conquest of the Desert took Patagonian lands from indigenous peoples.

history.heading: Boom, Perón and military rule
paragraphs: From the 1880s to 1930, Argentina became one of the world's richest countries by exporting beef and grain, attracting millions of immigrants, mainly from Italy and Spain. A military coup in 1930 began decades of instability.

Juan Domingo Perón, elected in 1946, built a powerful movement based on workers' rights and nationalism, with his wife Eva Perón as an iconic figure. He was overthrown in 1955. Alternating civilian and military governments culminated in the 1976–1983 dictatorship, during which thousands of people were "disappeared". Defeat in the 1982 Falklands War against Britain led to the return of democracy.

history.heading: Democracy and economic crises
paragraphs: Since 1983, Argentina has held regular democratic elections and prosecuted many crimes of the dictatorship. The economy, however, has gone through repeated crises, including hyperinflation in 1989–90 and a deep collapse in 2001–02 with a record debt default.

Politics in the 21st century has swung between Peronist governments and their opponents. In 2023, libertarian economist Javier Milei won the presidency promising radical cuts to public spending and an end to chronic high inflation.

culture.heading: A nation of immigrants
paragraphs: Most Argentines are of European descent, especially Italian and Spanish, with significant mestizo and indigenous populations, and communities of Middle Eastern, Jewish and other origins. Spanish is the official language, spoken with a distinctive accent and the "vos" form; Italian influence is visible in vocabulary and gestures.
Roman Catholicism is the largest religion; Pope Francis, the first pope from the Americas, was from Buenos Aires.

culture.heading: Tango, literature and the arts
paragraphs: Tango was born in the working-class neighbourhoods of Buenos Aires and Montevideo in the late 19th century and is recognised as intangible cultural heritage. Composers such as Carlos Gardel and Astor Piazzolla brought it to the world.

Argentine literature includes Jorge Luis Borges, Julio Cortázar and Ernesto Sabato, and the gaucho epic Martín Fierro. Buenos Aires has a lively theatre scene, and Argentine cinema has won two Academy Awards for best foreign-language film.

culture.heading: Food and football
paragraphs: Beef is central to Argentine cuisine, especially the asado, a social barbecue gathering. Other favourites include empanadas, milanesa, dulce de leche and Malbec wine from Mendoza. Drinking mate, a herbal tea shared from a gourd, is a daily ritual.

Football is a passion. Argentina has won the FIFA World Cup three times, in 1978, 1986 and 2022, and produced legends such as Diego Maradona and Lionel Messi. Polo, rugby and basketball are also popular.

politics.heading: Federal presidential republic
paragraphs: Argentina is a federal republic of 23 provinces and the Autonomous City of Buenos Aires. The president is elected directly for a four-year term, renewable once consecutively. Congress consists of a Chamber of Deputies and a Senate with three senators per province.
Peronism, a broad and flexible movement, has been the dominant force since the 1940s, opposed by coalitions of centre-right and liberal parties and, more recently, by Milei's libertarian movement.

politics.heading: Foreign policy
paragraphs: Argentina is a founding member of Mercosur and a member of the G20. It maintains its claim to the Falkland Islands (Islas Malvinas), South Georgia and the South Sandwich Islands, which are administered by the United Kingdom.
Relations with the International Monetary Fund, its largest creditor, are a recurring political issue.

economy.heading: Resources and agriculture
paragraphs: Argentina has abundant natural resources and fertile land. It is one of the world's largest exporters of soybeans and soy products, maize, wheat and beef. The Vaca Muerta formation in Patagonia holds some of the world's largest shale oil and gas reserves, and the northwest is rich in lithium.
Industry includes food processing, cars and chemicals, and the country has a well-educated workforce and a strong technology sector.

economy.heading: Instability
paragraphs: Despite its potential, Argentina's economy has been marked by high inflation, repeated debt defaults, currency controls and boom-and-bust cycles. The currency is the Argentine peso, and many Argentines save in US dollars.

Since 2023 the government has pursued sharp spending cuts, deregulation and a devaluation, which reduced inflation significantly while causing a painful recession and a rise in poverty in the short term.
